title: Probe result: raising inference max_size does not fix MOT20-06/08; it hurts
description:
## Question

mot-5zl showed MOT20-06 and MOT20-08 (1920x734, aspect 2.62) render at 1600x612 — a short side of 612 against a configured resolution of 1120. They are 40.5% of test frames. Could an inference-only max_size raise recover that, with no retrain?

## Answer: no. It degrades them, monotonically.

Three exports of the same I4 checkpoint (last_ema.pth, sha256 fb3f2f0d) over MOT20 test, differing only in model.max_size. Scored by coverage of MOT20's public det/det.txt at IoU>=0.5, our boxes at score>=0.5, every 20th frame. Public detections are not ground truth; this measures agreement, not quality.

| Sequence | max_size 1600 | 1920 | 2960 |
|---|---|---|---|
| MOT20-04 (control) | 0.977 | 0.976 | 0.976 |
| MOT20-06 | 0.815 | 0.815 | 0.753 |
| MOT20-07 | 0.951 | 0.951 | 0.946 |
| MOT20-08 | 0.754 | 0.749 | 0.703 |

Detection counts fall the same way (MOT20-06: 360,175 -> 350,622 -> 337,753) and peak confidence falls with them (MOT20-06 max score 0.9492 -> 0.9492 -> 0.9180).

Control that makes the comparison trustworthy: MOT20-04 (1545x1080) produces byte-identical output at 1920 and 2960 — 695,002 detections, max/frame 384 — because its long side never reaches either cap. The two runs differ only where they should.

Interpretation: the model was trained at max_size 1600. Running it at 2960 is geometry it never saw, and it degrades as out-of-distribution input normally does. Resolution at inference is not a free variable.

## Second result: the box-height gap was an artifact, not a bug

The earlier public-detection cross-check showed our median box height far below the public detector's on the wide sequences (MOT20-06: 141.4 vs 169.0; MOT20-08: 118.2 vs 159.0) while MOT20-04 matched almost exactly (169.8 vs 170.0). That looked like systematic height underestimation on 2.62-aspect sequences.

It is not. Those medians are over different populations: we emit ~350 boxes/frame, the public detector ~69, so our median sits deeper into small/distant people. Restricting to IoU>=0.5 MATCHED PAIRS, median per-pair height ratio ours/public:

| Sequence | matched pairs | ours | public | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MOT20-04 | 11,130 | 175.1 | 171.0 | 1.025 |
| MOT20-06 | 2,850 | 163.5 | 173.0 | 1.000 |
| MOT20-07 | 979 | 220.5 | 208.0 | 1.050 |
| MOT20-08 | 1,677 | 141.5 | 161.0 | 0.933 |

MOT20-06 is exactly 1.000. There is no height collapse on the wide sequences. Any analysis resting on the unmatched medians should be discarded.

## Third result: the 390-query budget is not the constraint

No frame in the test export reaches 389 detections at threshold 0.05 (max observed 386, MOT20-04). And MOT20 train ground truth tops out at 220 people per frame (MOT20-05); medians are 48/48/121/195 across MOT20-01/02/03/05. A budget of 390 is ample.

The reverse is the interesting part: we emit a MEDIAN of 363 boxes/frame on MOT20-06 at score>=0.05, against a public-detector median of 69 and a GT ceiling around 220. Most of that mass is low-confidence duplicates. That is a suppression problem, not a capacity or resolution problem, and it belongs to mot-3hs, mot-ov8 and mot-n2n.1.

## Artifacts

- finetuning/configs/rfdetr_2xl_i4-inference-probe-maxsize1920.toml and -maxsize2960.toml (inference-only; differ from the I4 config in exactly one value, verified by diff)
- artifacts/tracking/detections/rfdetr2xl-i4-e8-ms1920-t005/test/ and -ms2960-t005/test/
- artifacts/tracking/probe-crosscheck-rfdetr2xl-i4-e8-{t005,ms1920-t005,ms2960-t005}.json

## Limits

No ground truth exists on MOT20 test, so none of this measures accuracy. Coverage of a weaker detector is a proxy that can move for the wrong reasons. What it does support is a negative: there is no cheap inference-time win here, so the resolution question can only be settled by training at a raised max_size (mot-x82).
notes: Ran 2026-09-08 on GPU 7 while arm E occupied GPUs 0-6. This was a speculative probe I proposed, flagged to the user as droppable; it returned a clean negative plus two corrections to earlier readings, which is why it was worth the 30 minutes.
close_reason: Probe complete; the result is the deliverable. Answer is a clean negative: raising inference max_size degrades MOT20-06/08 monotonically (coverage 0.815->0.753 and 0.754->0.703), so there is no cheap inference-time fix. Two corrections to earlier readings are recorded in the description: the apparent box-height shortfall on wide sequences was a population artifact (matched-pair ratio is 1.000 on MOT20-06), and the 390-query budget is not binding. Full evidence in the description; artifacts listed there.

title: multi_scale is largely inert: the 1600 long-side cap collapses 8 requested scales to 1-2 for wide sequences
description:
## What

Every RF-DETR 2XL config in this project sets `multi_scale = true` with `resolution = 1120` and `max_size = 1600`. The intent is that each training image is resized to a short side drawn at random from 8 candidate scales, giving scale diversity across epochs.

For the widest sequences that does not happen. The long-side cap binds before the short side reaches its target, so most of the 8 scales render to the same pixel size and the random draw becomes a no-op.

## Mechanism

With `scale_jitter = false` (our setting) the train resize is option A only, from rfdetr/datasets/coco.py:675-683:

    SmallestMaxSize(max_size=<random draw from scales>)
    CappedLongestMaxSize(max_size=1600)

`CappedLongestMaxSize` clamps scale to <= 1.0, so it only ever shrinks. Once SmallestMaxSize has pushed the long side past 1600, the cap pulls the whole image back down, and every scale above that point lands on the same output. The wider the aspect ratio, the earlier this happens.

Because `scale_jitter = false`, option B (the SmallestMaxSize 400/500/600 -> RandomSizedCrop branch, which produces square outputs per scale and would restore diversity) is not in the pipeline at all. This finding depends on that setting; it would not hold with scale_jitter on.

## Measured

compute_multi_scale_scales(1120, expanded_scales=False, patch_size=16, num_windows=4) = [896, 960, 1024, 1088, 1152, 1216, 1280, 1344] — 8 scales.

Distinct rendered sizes actually reachable, per sequence:

| Sequence | Native | Aspect | Distinct of 8 | Rendered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MOT20-01 train | 1920x1080 | 1.78 | 2 | 1593x896, 1600x900 |
| MOT20-02 train | 1920x1080 | 1.78 | 2 | 1593x896, 1600x900 |
| MOT20-03 train | 1173x880 | 1.33 | 6 | 1194x896 .. 1600x1200 |
| MOT20-05 train | 1654x1080 | 1.53 | 4 | 1372x896 .. 1600x1045 |
| MOT20-04 test | 1545x1080 | 1.43 | 5 | 1282x896 .. 1600x1118 |
| MOT20-06 test | 1920x734 | 2.62 | 1 | 1600x612 |
| MOT20-07 test | 1920x1080 | 1.78 | 2 | 1593x896, 1600x900 |
| MOT20-08 test | 1920x734 | 2.62 | 1 | 1600x612 |

Reproduce: docker exec -w /media/data_2/opensource/mot-20 nvpt-dm .venv/bin/python, then compute_multi_scale_scales followed by f = s/min(w,h); f2 = min(1.0, 1600/max(w*f, h*f)).

## Why it matters

Two separate consequences, and they should not be conflated.

1. Training-time augmentation is weaker than the config implies. MOT20-01/02 — the 1920x1080 training sequences — see 2 of 8 scales. Only MOT20-03 gets most of the intended range, and it is the smallest-resolution sequence. So the scale augmentation this project believes it is buying is mostly being bought on one sequence.

2. Inference-time resolution on MOT20-06/08 is far below nominal. Those two render at 1600x612: a short side of 612 against a configured resolution of 1120, i.e. 55 percent of nominal. They are 40.5 percent of the test frames. Their 2.62 aspect ratio does not occur anywhere in the training set, whose widest is 1.78.

## Not yet established

That (2) actually costs accuracy. It is a plausible mechanism for a MOT20-06/08 deficit, but no measurement here separates it from the aspect ratio itself being out of distribution. mot-x82 (train at max_size 1920) is the clean test of the training side; an inference-only max_size raise is the cheap probe of the inference side.
notes: Found 2026-09-08 while investigating why the 21 hand-labelled MOT20-06/08 training frames did not help those sequences. Filed as bug rather than task because the config does not do what it says. No code change proposed yet: raising max_size raises memory and is a retrain, which is why it sits behind mot-x82.

title: export_detections.py crashes on a degenerate detection box
description:
Arm C's export died in validate_detections: "MOT20-03: frame 403 has a
degenerate box". A box with x2<=x1 or y2<=y1 has no usable geometry and would
corrupt downstream IoU, so the validator is right to reject it - but rejecting
it aborts the whole export after inference has already completed, wasting the
GPU pass.

Arms A and D never produced one, which is why this only surfaced when arm C was
first exported.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-09-08 in commit 53ff70f. export_detections.py now drops degenerate
boxes instead of aborting, and records how many.

The validator's judgement was correct and is unchanged - a zero or inverted
box is unusable. What changed is that the exporter filters them before
validation rather than letting a single bad box discard a completed GPU pass.

AGENTS.md permits dropping records; it forbids dropping them silently. So the
count is reported per sequence on the console line and stored as
degenerate_boxes_dropped in the detections manifest. The script already had
precedent for exactly this in its reported non-pedestrian drops.

Measured on the arm C re-run: 2 degenerate boxes across 1,328,762 detections,
one in MOT20-03 and one in MOT20-05. A rare edge case, now quantified rather
than assumed - which is the point of counting rather than silently filtering.

Provably a no-op for arms A and D: they passed the strict validator, so they
report a count of zero. I4's export subsequently reported zero as well.

Evidence: tracking/scripts/export_detections.py,
artifacts/tracking/detections/rfdetr2xl-armc-e9-t005/val_half/manifest.json,
artifacts/tracking/armc-export.log.

title: Separate training-data volume from density as the cause of duplicate set predictions
description:
mot-0p4 refuted CrowdHuman sparsity as the cause and produced a new lead: the
duplicate rate tracks TOTAL TRAINING IMAGES monotonically, not MOT20 share.

  4,489 imgs (arm C)   -> 48.984 dup/frame
  23,859     (arm A/D) -> 33.219 / 31.400
  28,322     (I4)      -> 28.923

That suggests incomplete convergence of the one-to-one assignment rather than
density or mixture composition. It is a correlation over four points, three of
which differ in other ways too.

Confounds still open:
- Arm C ran a different schedule (100 epochs, peak at 9) and a different
  effective batch. Volume and schedule are not separated.
- I4's point is contaminated: it trained on the frames it is measured on, so
  cleaner predictions are expected for free. Its 28.9 cannot be read as a clean
  data-volume effect.
- Density has NOT been isolated either. No arm has varied density independently
  of volume.

Do:
1. Add a GT-matched duplicate metric to analyze_detections.py: Hungarian-match
   predictions to ground truth and count multiple predictions assigned to one
   GT, across score thresholds. The current metric counts raw prediction pairs;
   analyze_gt_overlap.py bounds the confound at 0.585/frame but does not remove
   it. External review raised this and it is still outstanding.
2. Design one arm that varies training volume with schedule held fixed, or
   measure the duplicate rate per epoch on an existing run to see whether it
   falls with training progress. The second is nearly free and would test the
   convergence reading directly - arm E is checkpointing every epoch, so its
   checkpoints can supply that curve without a new training run.

Discovered from mot-0p4, 2026-09-08.
Evidence: docs/experiment-report.md section 2.3, docs/results-reference.md
sections 1.2b and 4.1.
notes:
PART 1 DONE (GT-matched duplicate metric). Part 2 (per-epoch curve) NOT started.

Implemented in tracking/scripts/analyze_detections.py:
  _cross_iou(), gt_matched_duplicates(), gt_matched_duplicates_multi()
  new args --gt-match-iou (default 0.5), --gt-duplicate-thresholds (default 0.05 0.10 0.20 0.50)
  report format bumped to mot20.tracking.detection-analysis.v2
Predictions are matched to GT at IoU >= 0.5, highest score first, one GT per
prediction. "redundant" = predictions matched to an already-covered GT, so two
overlapping PEOPLE can no longer be counted as a duplicate. That removes the
confound external review raised.

Artifact: artifacts/tracking/detection-analysis-gtdup-val_half.json
Split val_half, 4463 frames, 615137 GT boxes, maxDets 390, run 2026-09-07 21:13-23:31.

Result at score >= 0.05 (variants are the -t005 supersets, NO NMS):

  variant                  train imgs   pairwise/fr   GTdup/fr   per covGT   GT recall
  rfdetr2xl-armb-e1-t005            -        45.092     77.616      0.5795      0.9717
  rfdetr2xl-armc-e9-t005         4489        48.984     75.799      0.5669      0.9700
  rfdetr2xl-armd-e9-t005        23859        31.400     60.982      0.4546      0.9733
  rfdetr2xl-e5-t005             23859        33.219     63.666      0.4761      0.9703
  yoloxx20                          -         0.000      0.219      0.0018      0.9003

FINDING 1 - the confound was real but harmless in direction. The GT-anchored
count is roughly 1.9x the pairwise count, not lower. The two metrics use
different thresholds and measure different things: pairwise required mutual
IoU >= 0.75 between predictions, GT-matched requires IoU >= 0.5 to the same GT.
Two boxes can both cover one person at 0.5+ while overlapping each other below
0.75, and the old metric missed exactly those. Duplication was UNDERSTATED.

FINDING 2 - the mot-0p4 lead survives, with one qualification. The 4489-image
group (armb, armc: 75.8-77.6) stays clearly separated from the 23859-image
group (armd, e5: 61.0-63.7) under the cleaner metric, so the volume correlation
is not an artifact of the pairwise definition. But the within-group order flips
(pairwise put armc above armb, GT-matched puts armb above armc), so that pair is
not separated by either metric. The confounds listed in this issue - arm C's
different schedule, I4's contamination, density never isolated - are all
untouched by this work.

FINDING 3 - not a recall tradeoff. GT recall is 0.970-0.973 for all four RF-DETR
variants, spread 0.003. The duplicate difference is redundancy, not coverage.

FINDING 4 - yoloxx20 is NOT a valid comparator here and should not be quoted as
one. Its detections already went through YOLOX's own NMS; the -t005 RF-DETR
variants are raw query outputs with no NMS at all. Its 0 pairwise pairs at
IoU >= 0.75 is tautological (NMS removed them) and its 979 total GT-matched
redundant boxes follow from the same cause. It also recalls 7 points less GT
(0.9003 vs 0.973).

FINDING 5 - duplication is a low-threshold phenomenon. Redundant per covered GT
for armd: 0.4546 (t005) -> 0.2364 (t010) -> 0.0706 (t020) -> 0.0146 (t050).

title: Settle whether MOT20 density or CrowdHuman sparsity causes duplicate set predictions
description:
The phenomenon is established: arm A emits 33.219 overlapping pairs per frame at
IoU >= 0.75 in 4,463 of 4,463 frames, against a ground-truth person-on-person
overlap rate of 0.585 per frame (measured by `tracking/scripts/analyze_gt_overlap.py`,
`artifacts/tracking/gt-overlap-val_half.json`). So ~32.6 pairs per frame are not
explainable by real crowding, and NMS at IoU 0.70 removes them for +0.63 HOTA.

The *cause* is not established. `docs/experiment-report.md` section 2.3 offers
MOT20's density (137.8 instances/image, ~19x COCO) as the leading hypothesis,
but the competing hypothesis is that 81% of training images averaging 22.7
persons taught the Hungarian matching to expect sparsity. Both arms measured so
far are CrowdHuman-heavy, so they cannot separate the two.

Do: export arm C's detections. Arm C trained on MOT20 only with no CrowdHuman,
so its duplicate rate is the discriminating measurement. If arm C duplicates at
the same rate, density is implicated and CrowdHuman is exonerated; if it drops
sharply, the training mix is the cause and the fix is a data question rather
than an architectural one.

Also worth adding to `analyze_detections.py`: match predictions to GT and count
predictions-per-GT directly, rather than counting raw prediction pairs. The GT
control bounds the confound but does not remove it.

Blocked by nothing; arm C's checkpoint exists. Discovered by external review,
2026-09-08.
Evidence: `docs/experiment-report.md` section 2.3, `docs/results-reference.md`.

contradicts this project's own finding that mAP is not a sufficient selection
signal: NMS at IoU 0.70 lowers mAP@50:95 (0.6337 -> 0.6297) while raising HOTA
(68.175 -> 68.809), and the detection and tracking matrices disagree outright
for arm D.

notes:
STATE 2026-09-08. Partially unblocked: arm C's detections now exist.

Already done, via mot-0p4:
  artifacts/tracking/detections/rfdetr2xl-armc-e9-t005/  (geometry checksum
  expected 0.6139 observed 0.6143 MATCH; 2 degenerate boxes dropped, recorded)

Remaining for arm C: derive_filtered_variant.py to -t010-nms070, OSNet
embeddings (GPU, ~1.2GB), run_boosttrack.py, evaluate_tracks.py. Tracking and
evaluation are CPU-only once embeddings exist.

Remaining for arm B: the whole chain, starting from export. Checkpoint is at
finetuning/artifacts/rfdetr-2xl-i5-armb-2026-09-07-r1/checkpoint_best_total.pth,
peak EMA 0.6168 at epoch 1 - pass --expected-map 0.6168 and its own config.

Why this still matters: the three-arm mix ablation was stopped at mAP because no
arm beat arm A, and docs/experiment-report.md flags that as an assumption never
tested. Arm D has since shown that detection and tracking metrics can disagree
sharply - it lost to YOLOX on mAP@50:95 while winning HOTA - so "no arm beat arm
A on mAP" does not establish that no arm would beat it on HOTA.

Note arm C is the weakest arm on every detection metric AND the worst
duplicator, so the expected outcome is that it loses on HOTA too. The value is
in testing the assumption, not in expecting a surprise.
close_reason:
Measured 2026-09-08. Arms B and C are now carried through to HOTA, and the issue's premise is confirmed: the mAP ranking and the HOTA ranking disagree.

All rows OSNet (held out), t010 + greedy NMS 0.70, BoostTrack++ defaults, vendored TrackEval, val_half:

| arm | best mAP@50:95 | HOTA | DetA | AssA | MOTA | IDF1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D (e9) | 0.6282 | 70.777 | 72.979 | 68.775 | 87.976 | 85.637 |
| A (e5) | 0.6202 | 68.809 | 71.928 | 65.965 | 86.883 | 83.255 |
| B (e1) | 0.6168 | **68.976** | 71.527 | **66.653** | 86.674 | 83.743 |
| C (e9) | 0.6139 | 68.477 | 71.373 | 65.839 | 86.615 | 83.366 |

rank by mAP:  D > A > B > C
rank by HOTA: D > **B > A** > C

THE INVERSION IS BETWEEN A AND B, AND THE SHARPER POINT IS ABOUT RESOLUTION, NOT DIRECTION. mAP put A ahead of B by 0.0034. Per mot-6po, arm A's own epoch-to-epoch noise SD is 0.0051 and arm B's is 0.0032, so that gap was never distinguishable from noise in the first place. B was deferred on a difference mAP could not resolve. HOTA then puts B ahead by 0.167. So the correct statement is not merely 'mAP disagrees with HOTA' but 'mAP was used to discriminate at a resolution it does not have'.

MECHANISM OF THE INVERSION. B has LOWER DetA than A (71.527 vs 71.928) and HIGHER AssA (66.653 vs 65.965). The association gain outweighs the detection loss. This is the same pattern as the RF-DETR-vs-yoloxx20 comparison in mot-5bt, where arm D trails the baseline on DetA and wins on AssA. Detection-only metrics keep missing the quantity that decides HOTA on this dataset.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE. Neither B nor C beats arm D on any metric, so the original deferral did not cost a better model. Arm C is last on both rankings, and its deferral was correct on both. The practical conclusion of I5 stands; the reasoning that produced it did not.

CONFOUND, stated because it limits the reading. Arms A, B and C were all exported at long-side cap 1333; arm D at 1600 (verified in each detections manifest's geometry block). title: I7b: determine why the EMA branch won in arm D but lost in arm A
description:
`use_ema = true` throughout, yet arm A promoted the regular branch (0.6202
against EMA's 0.6198) while arm D promoted EMA (0.6282 against regular's
0.6243, `best_total_source = ema` at global_step 3730).

So EMA was updating; the question is why the branches swapped. Answerable from
`metrics.csv` files already on disk, no GPU required.

Evidence: `docs/results-reference.md` sections 3.1 and 3.4.
close_reason:
I7b answered 2026-09-08, CPU only, from the stored metrics.csv files. The premise is wrong: EMA did not lose in arm A. The branch swap is a max-selection artifact, not a change in EMA behaviour.

EMA IS AHEAD ON AVERAGE IN EVERY ARM, INCLUDING A:

| arm | evals | mean(ema-reg) | median | epoch-to-epoch SD of regular | best-of margin | margin / SD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 50 | +0.0028 | +0.0025 | 0.0051 | -0.0004 | -0.07 |
| B | 15 | +0.0019 | +0.0015 | 0.0032 | +0.0020 | 0.64 |
| C | 20 | +0.0018 | +0.0019 | 0.0026 | +0.0021 | 0.80 |
| D | 15 | +0.0030 | +0.0026 | 0.0070 | +0.0039 | 0.55 |

In arm A the EMA branch is above the regular branch in 42 of 50 evaluations. Its mean advantage, +0.0028, is actually the second largest of any arm. Arm D's mean advantage is +0.0030 — statistically the same thing.

MECHANISM. Selection takes a max over both branches and all epochs. Arm A's regular branch happened to spike at epoch 5 to 0.6202, its single best value of the whole 50-epoch run, and epoch 5 is one of the eight evaluations where EMA was momentarily behind (-0.0010). EMA's own best, 0.6198, arrived at epoch 8. So the rule compared two independent noise peaks and the regular one was higher by 0.0004:

  e3 regular 0.6049 ema 0.6146 (+0.0097)
  e4 regular 0.6127 ema 0.6177 (+0.0050)
  e5 regular 0.6202 ema 0.6192 (-0.0010)   <- regular's global peak, EMA momentarily behind
  e6 regular 0.6141 ema 0.6197 (+0.0056)
  e8 regular 0.6149 ema 0.6198 (+0.0050)   <- EMA's global peak

That 0.0004 margin is -0.07 standard deviations of arm A's own epoch-to-epoch volatility (SD 0.0051), i.e. about one fourteenth of a typical step between consecutive evaluations. Nothing happened.

CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE QUESTION. Checkpoint selection is a max over roughly 2 x N noisy evaluations — 100 draws in arm A — against a metric whose per-epoch noise is 0.003 to 0.007 mAP depending on the arm. Selection is therefore biased upward and is not reliable at the 0.001 level. Two practical rules follow:

1. Do not treat a best_total_source of 'ema' or 'regular' as evidence about EMA. It is which noise peak was higher.
2. Do not read arm-to-arm differences below roughly 0.005 mAP@50:95 as real. Arm D's 0.6282 against arm A's 0.6202 is 0.008, about 1.6 SD, which is suggestive rather than decisive.

This also intersects I7: arm A's regular branch peaked at epoch 5 of 50 and never recovered, which is the decay pattern mot-ayx is chasing.

Note: the I4 run's metrics.csv carries no eval rows at all, because its valid split is deliberately empty (formal_empty_validation). Nothing to compare there, as designed.

title: Decision: whether to build a clean YOLOX baseline ourselves
description:
With MOT17 out of scope there is no held-out external baseline available, so
the yoloxx20 leakage caveat is permanent. The only in-scope remedy is training
YOLOX-X on mot20_train_half ourselves, which would give a genuinely held-out
comparison at the cost of a full training run on an architecture this project
does not otherwise maintain.

Not costed, not scheduled. Recorded so the caveat's only exit is visible.

Evidence: `docs/experiment-report.md` section 0.
notes:
STATE 2026-09-08. New evidence changes this decision's calculus in both
directions. Kept OPEN for discussion; not decided.

ARGUES AGAINST needing a clean baseline: I4 was measured on val_half as a
matched-contamination parity check (mot-n2n.2). Both I4 and yoloxx20 trained on
those frames, so that one comparison has no asymmetry - it is the condition
ByteTrack itself reports MOT20 numbers under. I4 won every metric there:
HOTA 75.865 vs 70.208, MOTA 91.986 vs 85.031, and every detection metric
including the two YOLOX had won held out. So we now have A comparison that is
symmetric, without training anything.

ARGUES FOR: that parity is only approximate. The two models saw val_half in
different proportions, for different epoch counts, under different
architectures. Nothing measures whether their contamination is equally large,
and the arm D -> I4 gap of +5.088 HOTA shows contamination is worth several
HOTA on our side alone. So the parity check bounds nothing.

ALSO RELEVANT, verified from the vendored source today: ByteTrack had no
validation data for its MOT20 model either. exps/example/mot/yolox_x_mix_mot20_ch.py
sets val_ann = "test.json" against the MOT20 TEST split, and
tools/convert_mot20_to_coco.py writes annotations only when split != 'test', so
that file has zero ground truth. Their trainer's best-checkpoint condition
(ap50 > best_ap, best_ap starting at 0) can therefore never fire. They trained a
fixed 80 epochs and took the final weights. Their only real held-out validation
is yolox_x_ablation.py on MOT17 half-split - a different dataset.

So a clean MOT20-trained YOLOX-X would not just be a baseline for us; it would
be something the ByteTrack authors never produced. That raises both its value
and its cost, and it is why this stays a decision rather than a task.
close_reason: Decided 2026-09-08 by user: not building a clean YOLOX baseline. Out of scope for this workstream, which is RF-DETR detector work only. Consequence accepted: the yoloxx20 leakage caveat on the external baseline is permanent and every comparison against it must continue to carry that caveat. Evidence: docs/experiment-report.md section 0.

title: Make NMS a first-class export option rather than a derived post-filter
description:
Greedy NMS at IoU 0.70 is the measured best export setting and is worth +0.63
HOTA, but it is applied today by `derive_filtered_variant.py` after the fact.
Future exports should carry it by default so the good setting is the path of
least resistance.

Engineering, not an experiment.

Evidence: `docs/tracker-improvements.md` section I1.
close_reason:
Done 2026-09-08. tracking/scripts/export_detections.py now takes --min-score and --nms-iou, so the measured-best export (score 0.10, greedy NMS at IoU 0.70) is producible in one step instead of by a second pass over written files.

DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM THE ISSUE, worth reading. The issue asked for NMS 'by default'. I made it first-class but left it OFF by default, because defaulting it on would break the artifact store's central invariant. L1 detections are exported below any tracker threshold on purpose: BoostTrack boosts low-confidence detections that match existing tracks BEFORE applying its own cut, so a pre-filtered file silently disables that mechanism. A filtered variant can always be derived from an unfiltered one; the reverse is impossible. Making filtering the default would make the base artifact lossy and every derivation one-way. The intent of the issue — the good setting should not require a second script — is met; the default is not, and the reasoning is now in the module docstring so the choice is not re-litigated from scratch.

GUARD ADDED that is arguably the more valuable half. Every artifact path and cache key derives from the variant slug, so a filtered export written under a raw-looking name is indistinguishable from a raw one forever afterwards. _require_slug_declares_filtering refuses to write unless the slug encodes what was applied, following the existing convention (score x100 zero-padded, IoU x100 zero-padded: rfdetr2xl-i4-e8-t010-nms070). Two further guards: --nms-iou must be in (0, 1], and --min-score below the capture threshold is refused because it would imply a completeness the export does not have.

REFACTOR. greedy_nms moved from tracking/scripts/derive_filtered_variant.py into tracking/src/mot20_tracking/detections.py, where the rest of the L1 contract lives, and both scripts now import the one copy. Filter order inside the export is degenerate-box drop, then score, then NMS — suppression decided among boxes that survive, not by boxes about to be discarded — and the manifest records score_filtered, nms_suppressed, and a lossless flag.

VERIFIED, not assumed:
- greedy_nms unit behaviour after the move: two overlapping plus one disjoint box gives 2 survivors at IoU 0.70 and 3 at 0.99; empty input returns an empty mask.
- BEHAVIOUR PRESERVED BYTE FOR BYTE: re-derived rfdetr2xl-i4-e8-t010-nms070 on the test split through the moved function and all four sequence det.txt files are sha256-identical to the originals. The verification variant was then deleted.
- All four guards fire with correct messages, including the slug convention suggestion (-t010, -nms070).
- derive_filtered_variant.py still runs after losing its local copy.

Note for whoever reads a filtered manifest: --expected-map checksums the library's evaluation, which runs BEFORE this filtering, so it remains a valid check on export geometry but does not describe the filtered file. That is stated in the docstring.

description:

METHOD NOTE worth reusing. Rather than one GPU embedding pass per sweep point, OSNet embeddings were computed ONCE over the t005 superset (1,261,854 rows, ~50 min on one GPU). Every sweep point is a subset of that, so derive_filtered_variant.py --reid selects the rows with no ReID forward passes and the entire sweep ran on CPU. Nine points cost one GPU job.

NMS IoU sweep, min-score fixed at 0.10:

| NMS IoU | rows | HOTA | DetA | AssA | MOTA | IDF1 | IDSW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | 958,353 | 69.825 | 73.107 | 66.836 | 88.059 | 83.854 | 1763 |
| 0.60 | 809,393 | 69.508 | 71.928 | 67.303 | 86.694 | 84.483 | 1228 |
| **0.70** | 873,131 | **70.777** | 72.979 | 68.775 | 87.976 | 85.637 | 1262 |
| 0.75 | 900,549 | 70.513 | 73.139 | 68.119 | 88.160 | 85.078 | 1333 |

Clean single peak at 0.70, confirming the value adopted from the e5 sweep now that it has been re-measured on arm D rather than assumed to transfer. Range across the sweep is 1.27 HOTA, so this knob matters.

Note what the detection-side metrics say: DetA and MOTA both peak at IoU 0.80 (73.243 and 88.222), where HOTA is 0.41 WORSE. AssA peaks at 0.70 and carries HOTA with it. Tuning this on DetA or MOTA would pick the wrong operating point. That is the third independent instance today of association, not detection, deciding the outcome (see mot-0e9 and mot-5bt).

Threshold sweep, NMS IoU fixed at 0.70:

| min-score | rows | HOTA | DetA | AssA | MOTA | IDF1 | IDSW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 1,079,348 | 70.688 | 72.990 | 68.592 | 87.982 | 85.469 | 1256 |
| 0.10 | 873,131 | 70.777 | 72.979 | 68.775 | 87.976 | 85.637 | 1262 |

RECOMMENDATION, with its own caveat. Adopt min-score 0.15 with NMS IoU 0.70 for arm D. It is also 12% cheaper: 766,845 rows against 873,131 for the current setting, so fewer boxes to embed and track. But the honest reading is that threshold is nearly FLAT here — the whole sweep spans 0.195 HOTA, against 1.27 for NMS IoU. The +0.106 gain is real in the sense of reproducible (the pipeline is deterministic) but it is a single-split result on a nearly flat surface and should not be treated as a robust optimum. NMS IoU is the knob that matters; threshold anywhere in 0.10-0.20 is close to equivalent.

New artifacts: embeddings rfdetr2xl-armd-e9-t005__osnet-ain-msdc (the reusable superset), plus detections, derived embeddings, tracks and metrics for t010-nms060/075/080, t010 (no NMS), and t005/t015/t020-nms070.

title: Train at max_size 1920 for native scale
description:
Native 1920x1080 at roughly 2.1x arm A's pixels, likely needing micro-batch 4
with gradient checkpointing already on.

Expect little: arm D already matched the baseline's effective scale exactly
(0.833 against 0.830) and moved LocA by 0.131. Recorded so the option is not
re-proposed as novel.

Do not attempt this at inference only. Probes at caps 1600 and 1920 leave
recall flat (0.9134 -> 0.9138 -> 0.9167) while mAP@75 falls 0.7400 -> 0.5943 ->
0.6890; the model regresses boxes well only at its trained geometry.

Evidence: `docs/results-reference.md` section 4.3.
notes:
2026-09-08: mot-5zl gives this experiment a sharper motivation and a concrete prediction. At the current max_size=1600, MOT20-06/08 (1920x734, aspect 2.62) render at 1600x612 — a short side of 612 against the configured resolution of 1120. They are 40.5% of test frames. Raising max_size to 1920 would let them reach the nominal short side and would also restore most of the multi_scale range for the 1920x1080 sequences, which currently see only 2 of 8 scales. Prediction to check: if the deficit is a resolution effect, MOT20-06/08 improve most; if it is the out-of-distribution 2.62 aspect ratio itself, they improve least. See mot-5zl for the measured table.
2026-09-08 CORRECTION to the note above. I overstated the case for this experiment earlier today. mot-0s6 tested the inference-only version of the resolution hypothesis and it FAILED: running the 1600-trained I4 checkpoint at max_size 1920 and 2960 made MOT20-06/08 worse, not better (public-detection coverage 0.815 -> 0.815 -> 0.753 and 0.754 -> 0.749 -> 0.703), with peak confidence falling alongside.

That does not invalidate this bead — training at native scale is a different thing from running a 1600-trained model at a scale it never saw, and only training can settle it. But two supporting arguments I gave are now withdrawn:

1. The 'MOT20-06/08 boxes are systematically short' observation was a population artifact. On IoU>=0.5 matched pairs the median height ratio ours/public is 1.000 on MOT20-06 and 0.933 on MOT20-08. There is no height collapse to fix.
2. The 390-query budget is not a constraint either: no test frame reaches 389 detections, and train GT tops out at 220 people per frame.

What actually stands out instead is oversupply: a median of 363 boxes per frame on MOT20-06 at score>=0.05 against a GT ceiling near 220. That points at duplicate suppression (mot-3hs, mot-ov8, mot-n2n.1) rather than resolution. Weigh this bead's priority against those before spending 10-12 h of GPU on it.
